title: How do you tell if a browser prototype is worth continuing or just slop?
author: ke1lle
selftext:
Lately I've been cracking out rough browser prototypes lately, and the hard part is not getting something playable. it is figuring out if the thing is worth continuing or just AI slop with a play button.

half the time it looks like a game but plays like nothing. you waste a few nights tweaking controls, timing, tiny effects, then realize the core idea was the problem.

So heres my current filter, simple but brutal.

first: can someone get the goal in 30 seconds without me explaining it.

second: do they replay because they want to, not because i asked.

third: does it feel bad because the mechanic is boring, or because the juice is missing. boring mechanic is unfixable and bad juice is fixable.

how do you guys tell a bad prototype from a badly juiced prototype?Curious what your own filters look like.

comments.author: swirllyman
comments.body: Imo bad juice is fixable, bad core loop is not.

comments.author: bettertagsweretaken
comments.body:
If you require that everyone get to the core of your game within 30 seconds, you're never going to attempt a complicated game/engine/core idea, because sometimes it takes narrative or discovery or systems learning to get into it. 

Auto battlers, any game with a compelling story, etc. All of those are going to require some level of setup from the dev and patience from the user.

comments.author: blessed--
comments.body:
no time is wasted

every prototype counts towards the grander goal of making the magnum opus, IMO

I've cranked out like 5 low quality unity projects and a few i actually tried to do something beyond my ability

gotta learn your limits. yea theres a reason I cant quite make DMC yet lol. but I CAN make a dope ass RPG i believe

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
I feel you there. Great animations are not something AI can help me with yet, so a DMC style spectacle feels out of the question. 

But you CAN make a dope ass RPG. Maybe basic animations and such to start with, but some of the greatest RPGs didn't have amazing fighting graphics (BG 1 and 2, and all the related games.) Perfectly doable with modern tools.

replies.author: blessed--
replies.body: yea man i tried lol. i tried DMC, i tried a crazy platformer with states, i have TONS of asset store packs but nothing comes togther right. even tried fable to make a full character controller for walljumps, wallrunning, hanging, swinging on poles etc. but it broke apart. only so many shortcuts

comments.author: ishmaellius
comments.body:
I think it's just gotta be fun. 

I've been doing similar, and even at the prototype stage I don't get at least a little hooked into the core loop a little bit, it's probably a loser.

It doesn't take much to get enough to expose a core loop, but the challenge is you gotta see people playing again on their own, or at a minimum yourself.

I don't really think there's an alternative.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
Just read up on core game development. It's not any different using AI.

It changes a bit based on the type of game you're making but it mostly revolves around game loops and mechanics. Game mechanics need to feel good and feel fun to do, and game loops need to be rewarding and challenging enough to keep someone engaged but not difficult enough that it becomes tedious or frustrating. Everything after that is essentially the cherry on top.

Also when it comes to AI a game's aesthetics play a greater role. Anything that has obvious AI art is instantly going to put a lot of people off regardless of how good the gameplay is. It comes across as low effort.

comments.author: davesoft
comments.body: I'd judge it based on what's left to explore. I played with xcom stargate then stretched it to include puzzle and stealth mechanics, hit a wall of 'but these are just little scenarios, i want a big world' and started over, since xcom is not the interface for a big world. The xcom experiment is still live, and I'll refine it some more one day, but for now that experiment has proved it's point and I'm on to other experiments, same 'game' just everything is different :P

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
I think it helps to have a few "almost" ideas and prototypes for AI to draw on. Lately I've been having a lot of success with "let's do a variation on my game X, combining features of my games Y and Z." 

A good base of solid design and ideas you've already refined is a great way to segue into a new game based on those ideas. The AI has a good understanding of how those work, instead of trying to guess at your meaning. 

I've reused the same WebGPU tech for swarms, and Vertex Animated Textures for 3d rendering in the browser, for half a dozen further games. The Synthwave games I started formed the visual basis for new games using that swarm/VAT tech, and now I have even more cool ideas to try.

Ive got all my AI repos in one directory, and Claude can refer to any of them to reuse tech and code to build new games based on those proven prototypes.

replies.author: davesoft
replies.body:
I've found problems when splitting a repo's mind though, a real time version of the xcom experiment was noticable still turn based under the hood nomatter how much I tried smoothing it out, but then part of the prompt was to leave the original game intact. I should try 'make a new folder with x, use y as reference material', I bet that would work without blowing it's mind.

I havn't tried codex in unity yet, I hear it's not bad, but I can't fix everything in unity, whereas in js if I really have to I can drink a coffee and dive in and fix it myself. And I quite like the low poly models that codex tends to make in three.js, it's not like I'm going to sell any of the trash i make, it's all "holodeck, entertain me, but in precisely this way" :D

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
>noticable still turn based under the hood nomatter how much I tried smoothing it out

Diablo 1 started out like that. It can definitely work lol. 

And yeah sometimes the visuals impress me. Even just silly stuff like the AI putting cowboy hats and ninja hoods on the basic capsule added enough character to help. I certainly will replace those with actual models later, but for now it's actually sorta cute. That one is a remake of an old mod I helped with in 2007, Master Blasters, but the AI got the main ideas down quite well. I'll have to rerecord my voice lines lol. 

Even some of the procedural boxy knights Claude Fable has made work pretty well, and it did a great job of skeletal animating them too.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
Do you have a vision beyond the prototype? I have like 20 prototypes going right now, but they're just at small milestones to prove concepts. For me, a game has to have a clear hook and ways I can build upon it. I'm not trying to one shot prompt a finished game. 

But maybe you need to explore other ideas. It's taking me a while to settle on which games I want to work on.

Maybe you need to try designing a few games, and the one that sounds most exciting and has a clear hook could be the one you work on. For me, that's several games at once. And the list keeps growing because I can't stop thinking about cool ideas I'd love to see. 

Now the issue is more which game is the most exciting one to spend my time on. I know I have a few good concepts, but the ones that I keep getting inspiration for get the most work. Improvements they just have to have to be the game I want.

comments.author: Unfair-Frosting-4934
comments.body: It's all about depth, how much content is there really or is it hiding behind either nice art or repeat clicks or looping. I have a browser gaming website where we include free to play browser based games of **quality** . [slagdock.com](http://slagdock.com) you can check some of the titles ppl have made there. You can see its not just about the first initial gmeplay loop but the reward system and secondary features to your games.
